0.title: Pictures of the Church
0.essay:
Ask a group of people what comes to mind when they hear the word “church”, and you will hear about buildings, steeples, services, rotas, perhaps a disappointment or two. Ask the New Testament, and it answers with pictures: a body, a bride, a temple, a flock, a family, a vine, a city shining on a hill. Before it gives us a definition, it gives us something to look at.

Why look again?

Many Christians love Jesus and feel lukewarm about the church. Some have been hurt by it. Some treat it as a service provider, to be used when it suits. Some simply have never been shown how highly God thinks of it. Paul speaks of “the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood” (Acts 20:28). That is what it cost. A people bought at that price cannot be a small thing to God, and should not be a small thing to us.

The Bible’s pictures reach the heart and the imagination as well as the mind. A body makes us feel that we need one another; a bride, that we are loved; a family, that we are at home. And each picture says something about Christ, because the church is never described on its own. It is always his body, his bride, his flock.

What this study does

This study takes the great pictures one or two at a time. For each, it asks where the picture comes from in the Old Testament, what it meant to the first Christians who heard it, what it shows us of Christ, what it says about us, and what difference it makes on an ordinary Sunday and Monday. Along the way it meets some honest objections, such as the church’s failures and the question of Israel and the church.

The study The Church sets out what the church is, how it is led and how it keeps the ordinances; Union with Christ (its chapter “Vine, Body and Bride”) looks at several of these pictures as pictures of our union with him; God with His People traces the temple from the garden to the city; and The Lord Is My Shepherd explores the shepherd. This study goes deeper into each picture of the church itself.

The chapters

Why So Many Pictures?; A People and a Holy Nation; The Body of Christ; The Bride of Christ; The Temple of the Living God; The Household and Family of God; The Flock and Its Shepherd; Vine, Olive Tree and Field; Salt, Light, Letters and Exiles; and The Church at the End: Bride and City.

For reflection

When you hear the word “church”, what picture comes to mind first, and where did it come from? Which of the pictures listed above do you know least well, and which would you most like to be true of your own church?

1.title: Why So Many Pictures?
1.essay:
If you wanted to describe your mother to a stranger, you would not give a single fact. You would tell stories, mention her laugh, describe her kitchen, recall something she once said. Some realities are too rich for one description. The church is one of them, and so the New Testament gives us not one picture but many.

Nearly a hundred images

Scholars who have counted the images of the church in the New Testament have found close to a hundred. Some are famous: the body, the bride, the temple, the flock. Others are easy to miss: salt, a letter, a field, a lampstand, an army, a holy priesthood, exiles, a pillar, a new humanity. Many of them appear in a single breath. In one paragraph Peter calls believers living stones, a spiritual house, a holy priesthood, a holy nation and sojourners (1 Peter 2:4–11). Paul can move from citizens to family to building to temple in three verses (Ephesians 2:19–22).

This is not untidy thinking. God himself is shown to us as rock, shepherd, father, king and husband, as the study Pictures of God explores, and each picture corrects the others. The same is true of the church.

Why no single picture is enough

Every picture shows something and leaves something out. A body shows unity and variety, but a body does not choose to belong. A bride shows love and intimacy, but says little about how many members the church has. A temple shows holiness and God’s presence, but stones do not love one another. A flock shows our dependence, but sheep are not known for their gifts. A family shows warmth and belonging, but families are born, while the church is born again.

So the pictures need each other. If we hold only one, we will bend the church out of shape. A church that thinks of itself only as a family may become cosy and inward. A church that thinks of itself only as an army may become harsh and driven. A church that thinks only of the temple may forget the warmth of the household. The whole set keeps us balanced.

The word itself

Even the word “church” carries a picture. The Greek word ekklēsia meant an assembly, a gathering of people called together. In Greek cities it was used of the citizens’ assembly. But the Greek translation of the Old Testament, which the first Christians read, had already used it for Israel gathered before God. Stephen speaks of Moses and “the congregation in the wilderness” (Acts 7:38). When Jesus said, “I will build my church” (Matthew 16:18), his hearers would have thought of Israel at Sinai: a people summoned by God’s voice to stand in his presence. The church is the people God calls and gathers to himself.

Pictures shape how we feel

Our pictures of church shape our feelings about it, whether we notice or not. If your picture is a building, church is a place you go. If your picture is a business, you are a customer, and you leave when the service is poor. If your picture is a club, you join people like you. If your picture is a hospital for the sick, you may feel welcome but never expect to grow strong enough to help others.

Timothy Keller often pointed out that people today tend to think of church as one more voluntary association we join for our own benefit, and that this quietly makes us consumers of it. The Bible’s pictures will not let us do that. You do not join a body as a customer. You do not attend a family. A bride is not a member of a service. The pictures retrain our hearts, so that we feel about the church more as God does.

Always Christ’s

Notice one thing in every picture. The church is never the main character. It is the body of Christ, the bride of Christ, the temple where Christ is the cornerstone, the flock of the good Shepherd, the branches of the true vine, the household of the Father where Christ is the firstborn among many brothers. Remove Christ, and every picture collapses: a body without a head, a bride with no groom, a building with no foundation.

That is a great comfort when the church disappoints us. Its worth does not rest on its performance. It rests on whose it is. The church is precious because Christ is precious, and because he has bound himself to it. To look closely at these pictures is, in the end, to look at him.

For us

Before reading further, notice your own picture of church. Is it a building, a weekly event, an organisation, a duty? Ask God to replace it, picture by picture, with his.

An example

A man in his forties has gone to the same church for years, and thinks of it as he thinks of his gym: useful, sometimes tiresome, easily replaced. A small group studies Ephesians, and he notices that Paul never once describes the church as something you use. The phrase “members one of another” stays with him. The next month he notices an older member who has stopped coming, and for the first time he feels it as a loss to himself. He calls round.

For reflection

Which picture of church have you carried without realising it: building, business, club, or something else? Why do you think God gives many pictures rather than one definition? Which of the pictures named in this chapter is newest to you? How does it change your view of church to see that every picture is centred on Christ?

2.title: A People and a Holy Nation
2.essay:
The first picture is the simplest and the oldest. Before the church is a body, a bride or a temple, it is a people: a nation that God made for himself, out of nothing, to show the world what he is like.

The Old Testament roots

The picture begins with a promise to Abraham, that through him “all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis 12:3). It takes shape at Sinai. God has just brought Israel out of slavery, and before he gives a single commandment he tells them who they are: “you shall be my treasured possession among all peoples, for all the earth is mine; and you shall be to me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation” (Exodus 19:5–6).

Notice the order: God rescues, and then he calls. And notice the reason. It was not because Israel was impressive: “It was not because you were more in number than any other people that the LORD set his love on you and chose you, for you were the fewest of all peoples, but it is because the LORD loves you” (Deuteronomy 7:7–8). The only explanation for the people of God is the love of God.

Israel was meant to be a priestly nation, standing between God and the nations, showing them the Lord. Too often it failed. Through Hosea God even named one of the prophet’s children “Not My People” (Hosea 1:9). Yet in the same breath he promised that “in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ it shall be said to them, ‘Children of the living God’” (Hosea 1:10).

What it meant to the first readers

Peter wrote to scattered churches in what is now Turkey, many of them Gentiles who had once worshipped idols. Into their ears he poured Israel’s titles: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession, that you may proclaim the excellencies of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light. Once you were not a people, but now you are God’s people” (1 Peter 2:9–10).

Imagine hearing that as a former pagan, perhaps a slave, mocked by your family for following a crucified Jew. You had no people. Now you belong to the oldest story in the world, and Hosea’s promise has come true in you (Romans 9:25–26).

What it says about Christ

How can Gentiles inherit Israel’s titles? Because of Christ, the true Israel, the one faithful Son. Abraham’s promised offspring is Christ, and “if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise” (Galatians 3:29). Christ has broken down “the dividing wall of hostility” and made Jew and Gentile into “one new man” (Ephesians 2:14–15). He “gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people for his own possession” (Titus 2:14). The church is a nation because it has a King, and its citizenship was bought with his blood.

Where Christians differ: Israel and the church

How does the church relate to Israel? Two main answers are held by sincere believers.

Covenant theology sees one people of God through all of history, under one covenant of grace. Believing Israel was the church in its childhood; at Pentecost it came of age and opened its doors to the nations. The promises to Israel are fulfilled in Christ and shared by all who belong to him, Jew and Gentile. Paul’s phrase “the Israel of God” (Galatians 6:16) means the whole believing people.

Dispensationalism, which grew from the teaching of John Nelson Darby in the nineteenth century and was spread widely by the Scofield Reference Bible, holds that Israel and the church are two distinct peoples with distinct programmes. God’s promises of land and kingdom to Israel will be fulfilled to the Jewish nation in a future earthly kingdom, and the church is a new people that began at Pentecost. More recent “progressive” dispensationalists see more continuity, but still expect a distinct future for national Israel. At its best this view guards something precious: God keeps his promises to Abraham’s physical descendants, and Christians must never treat the Jewish people with contempt. The study Dispensational Distinctives sets it out in its own terms.

This commentary’s view: there is one people of God across history, one olive tree into which believing Gentiles are grafted (Romans 11:17–24). This is fulfilment, not replacement. The church does not push Israel aside; it is Israel’s own hope come true in Israel’s Messiah, with the nations welcomed in. And with humility, this commentary reads Romans 11 as looking for a future turning of many Jewish people to Christ, within that one people. Christians should love the Jewish people and pray for their salvation. The study Covenant Theology says more.

What it says about us

To be a people means that our faith is never merely private. We were saved into a nation, not a waiting room of individuals. To be holy means set apart for God. To be priests means that every believer may come to God through Christ and that every believer is to bring others near to him. And the purpose matters: we are a people “that you may proclaim the excellencies of him who called you” (1 Peter 2:9). The holy nation exists to advertise its King.

For us

Next time you gather with your church, look around and say quietly: these are my people, not because we are alike, but because God called each of us out of darkness. Then ask how your church could show its neighbourhood something of his excellencies.

An example

A woman who came to faith as a refugee had lost her country, her language and most of her family. In a small church in a northern town she struggled to feel she belonged. One Sunday the pastor read 1 Peter 2:10. Afterwards she said, “I had no people. Now I am in the oldest nation in the world.” The congregation began to learn her name properly, and to ask about her story.

For reflection

Why does it matter that God called Israel “a holy nation” before he gave the law? What would it have meant to Peter’s first readers to be told, “now you are God’s people”? How does Romans 11 help us hold together the one people of God and a love for the Jewish people? In what ways is your faith more private than God intends?

3.title: The Body of Christ
3.essay:
Paul’s favourite picture of the church is the human body. It is so familiar that we can miss how daring it is. He does not say the church is like a body, or that Christians are like a club with Christ as its president. He says, “Now you are the body of Christ and individually members of it” (1 Corinthians 12:27).

Roots and background

The Old Testament has no direct picture of Israel as a body, though it often treats the people as one, standing or falling with their head, whether Adam or a king. In Paul’s world the body was a well-known political image. The Roman historian Livy tells how, when the common people of Rome once walked out of the city in protest, a senator named Menenius Agrippa won them back with a fable: the limbs rebelled against the belly, refused to feed it, and wasted away themselves. The moral was plain. Know your place; the lower orders exist to serve the whole.

Paul takes the same picture and turns it upside down. In his body, God has given “greater honor to the part that lacked it, that there may be no division in the body, but that the members may have the same care for one another” (1 Corinthians 12:22–25). The body of Christ is not a hierarchy that keeps the weak in their place. It is a body in which the weak are honoured.

What it meant in Corinth

The church in Corinth was gifted and proud. Some members, probably those with the more striking gifts, looked down on others. Some felt they did not matter at all. Paul speaks to both. To the ones who feel useless: “If the foot should say, ‘Because I am not a hand, I do not belong to the body,’ that would not make it any less a part of the body” (1 Corinthians 12:15). To the ones who feel superior: “The eye cannot say to the hand, ‘I have no need of you’” (1 Corinthians 12:21).

And he tells them how they got into the body: “For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, Jews or Greeks, slaves or free” (1 Corinthians 12:13). Nobody earned a place. The Spirit put each one there. That is why no member may despise another, and no member may despise himself.

What it says about Christ

In Colossians and Ephesians Paul adds the head: Christ “is the head of the body, the church” (Colossians 1:18). The head gives the body its life, its direction and its unity. From him “the whole body, joined and held together by every joint with which it is equipped, when each part is working properly, makes the body grow so that it builds itself up in love” (Ephesians 4:16). There is one head, and he is in heaven. No pastor, bishop or denomination takes his place.

The picture also shows how closely Christ binds himself to us. When Saul of Tarsus was hunting Christians, the risen Lord stopped him with the words, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). Not “my followers”, but “me”. A head feels what is done to its body. When a believer is in prison in a far country, or weeping alone in a flat in your own town, Christ is not a distant observer. He “nourishes and cherishes” the church, Paul says, as a man cares for his own flesh, “because we are members of his body” (Ephesians 5:29–30).

Think what that means. The eternal Son, through whom all things were made, has joined a ragged company of forgiven sinners to himself so closely that Scripture calls them his body. He feels their pain, and he will not lose a single part.

What it says about us

First, we belong. A hand cut off from the body does not become a free hand; it becomes a dead one. Christian faith is personal, but it is never solitary.

Second, we differ. “For as in one body we have many members, and the members do not all have the same function” (Romans 12:4). God “arranged the members in the body, each one of them, as he chose” (1 Corinthians 12:18). Some teach, some serve, some give, some pray quietly for years, known only to God. Comparing ourselves with others is like an ear envying an eye.

Third, we need one another. Christ gave teachers “to equip the saints for the work of ministry, for building up the body of Christ” (Ephesians 4:12). The ministry is the work of the whole body, not a few professionals.

Fourth, we suffer and rejoice together. “If one member suffers, all suffer together; if one member is honored, all rejoice together” (1 Corinthians 12:26). In a healthy church, one family’s grief becomes everyone’s concern, and one person’s answered prayer becomes everyone’s joy.

An objection

Someone may say, “I have been hurt by the body. It did not care for its weaker members; it ignored me.” That can be painfully true, and if there has been abuse, safety comes first and it must be reported to the authorities. But notice that Paul’s picture is a rebuke to such a church, not a defence of it. The body Christ intends is the one where the weak are honoured. The answer to a sick body is not to amputate yourself, but, where you can, to find a healthier part of the body, and to pray that Christ, the head, will heal what is broken.

For us

Ask two questions this week. Which part of the body am I, and am I working properly? And who in my church is a “weaker” part, easily overlooked, whom I could honour?

An example

A young man with a learning disability puts out the chairs every Sunday. For years nobody thought much about it. One week he is in hospital, and the chairs are late and nobody is at the door to greet visitors. The elders realise how much he has quietly carried. The following Sunday the pastor thanks him publicly, reading 1 Corinthians 12:22. He beams for the rest of the morning.

For reflection

How does Paul’s use of the body picture differ from the Roman one? Are you more tempted to say “I do not belong” or “I have no need of you”? What does Acts 9:4 tell you about how Christ feels the sufferings of his people? Who in your church is a “weaker” member you could honour this month?

4.title: The Bride of Christ
4.essay:
Of all the pictures of the church, this is the most tender. The church is not only a people Christ rules, or a body he directs. She is a bride he loves. The Bible’s story begins with a wedding in a garden and ends with a wedding in a city, and the church is the bride.

The Old Testament roots

Long before Paul, the prophets spoke of the Lord as Israel’s husband. “For your Maker is your husband, the LORD of hosts is his name” (Isaiah 54:5). Jeremiah remembers Israel’s first love in the wilderness: “I remember the devotion of your youth, your love as a bride” (Jeremiah 2:2). Isaiah promises a day when the forsaken city will be renamed: “as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you” (Isaiah 62:5).

The picture is sharpest, and most painful, in Hosea. God told the prophet to marry a woman who would be unfaithful, and then, when she had left him, to go and bring her back: “Go again, love a woman who is loved by another man and is an adulteress, even as the LORD loves the children of Israel, though they turn to other gods” (Hosea 3:1). Israel’s idolatry is adultery. Yet God does not give her up. “I will betroth you to me forever. I will betroth you to me in righteousness and in justice, in steadfast love and in mercy” (Hosea 2:19).

What it meant to the first readers

In the ancient world a betrothal was a binding promise, much stronger than an engagement today. The bride waited, and the bridegroom came to fetch her for the wedding and the feast. The customs of betrothal and wedding stand behind Paul’s words to the Corinthians: “I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:2). The church now lives in the time of betrothal: promised, bound, loved, and waiting for her bridegroom to come.

Jesus called himself the bridegroom. When people asked why his disciples did not fast, he answered, “Can the wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them?” (Mark 2:19). John the Baptist described himself as “the friend of the bridegroom”, rejoicing at his voice (John 3:29). For Jewish hearers who knew Isaiah and Hosea, this was startling. Jesus was taking the role the prophets gave to the Lord himself.

What it says about Christ

Paul’s great passage on marriage turns out to be about something greater: “Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, that he might sanctify her, having cleansed her by the washing of water with the word, so that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle or any such thing” (Ephesians 5:25–27). Then he quotes Genesis about the two becoming one flesh and says, “This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church” (Ephesians 5:32).

Notice what kind of bridegroom this is. In most love stories the bride is chosen because she is beautiful. Here the bridegroom makes her beautiful. He finds her stained and unfaithful, and he does not wait for her to clean herself up. He gives himself up for her. He washes her. He will present her in splendour. Her beauty on the wedding day will be the work of his love from first to last.

Human marriage, Paul is saying, was designed from the beginning as a small copy of this great original. Every faithful marriage is a living parable; every wedding, however simple, points beyond itself.

What it says about us

This picture speaks of love. Many Christians believe that Christ tolerates them, or puts up with them for the Father’s sake. The bride picture says something stronger: he delights in his people. The church is not a project he manages but a bride he cherishes.

It speaks of purity. A betrothed bride keeps herself for her husband. Idolatry, whether of money, success, comfort or another person, is spiritual unfaithfulness, as Hosea saw. The bride is called to a single-hearted love.

It speaks of hope. The wedding has not yet happened. One day a voice like the roar of many waters will cry, “Let us rejoice and exult and give him the glory, for the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his Bride has made herself ready” (Revelation 19:7). And the angel says, “Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Revelation 19:9).

The picture is about the church together. Christ has one bride, not millions. Yet each of us is loved within her.

A word for the hurt and the single

Some readers have known betrayal in marriage, or long for a marriage that has not come, or are widowed. The bride picture is not a cruel reminder. It is a promise that the deepest longing beneath every human love will be met. The single Christian is not on the edge of this story; she or he is part of the bride, and will be at the wedding. The study Singleness says more.

For us

Read Ephesians 5:25–27 slowly and put “his people, including me” where it says “the church”. Then ask what idols are competing for the love that belongs to him, and turn back to the one who has never stopped loving his bride.

An example

An older woman, married for fifty years, sits by her husband’s bed as he dies. Afterwards, at the funeral, the minister reads Revelation 19. Over tea she tells a younger friend, “Our marriage was good, but it was only ever a picture. I think I am beginning to see what it was a picture of.” She grieves deeply, and she also looks forward.

For reflection

What does Hosea teach about God’s faithfulness to an unfaithful people? How is Christ different from every human bridegroom in Ephesians 5:25–27? Do you think of Christ as tolerating you or delighting in you, and why? What would it look like for your church to live as a bride waiting for her bridegroom?

5.title: The Temple of the Living God
5.essay:
For a thousand years, if you wanted to be near the living God, you went to one place: the temple in Jerusalem. Then the New Testament says something astonishing to a small group of ordinary believers in a pagan port city: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you?” (1 Corinthians 3:16).

The Old Testament roots

The whole Bible is a story of God coming to live with his people. In Eden he walked with Adam and Eve. At Sinai he said, “let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst” (Exodus 25:8). Solomon built the temple, and even as he dedicated it he marvelled: “But will God indeed dwell on the earth? Behold, heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you; how much less this house that I have built!” (1 Kings 8:27). The study God with His People traces this whole story, and Reading the Old Testament Well explains the tabernacle in detail.

The temple was the place of God’s presence, of sacrifice, of priests and of holiness. It was also, sadly, the place Israel defiled, and the glory left it before the Babylonians destroyed it. When it was rebuilt, the prophets promised a greater glory to come: “The latter glory of this house shall be greater than the former” (Haggai 2:9).

Christ the true temple

That greater glory came in a person. “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), literally “pitched his tent” among us. Jesus said, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19), and John explains, “he was speaking about the temple of his body” (John 2:21). In Jesus, God was living among his people in a way the old temple only pictured. And his body was destroyed on the cross, the true sacrifice to which every altar pointed, and raised on the third day.

What it meant to the first readers

The Corinthians lived in a city crowded with temples to many gods. In Paul’s question, “you are God’s temple”, the Greek the “you” is plural. He is not first speaking about each believer’s body (he does that later, in 1 Corinthians 6:19), but about the whole congregation gathered together. When this quarrelling church met in someone’s house, that room was holier than any shrine in Corinth, because the Spirit of God was among them. And so Paul adds a warning: “If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy him. For God’s temple is holy, and you are that temple” (1 Corinthians 3:17). Those who tear churches apart by pride and division are damaging something God regards as holy.

In Ephesians, writing to Gentiles who had been kept out of the temple courts by a dividing wall, Paul says they are now part of the building: “built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone, in whom the whole structure, being joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord. In him you also are being built together into a dwelling place for God by the Spirit” (Ephesians 2:20–22). The outsiders are now the sanctuary.

Living stones and the cornerstone

Peter, whose name means “rock”, loved this picture. “As you come to him, a living stone rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen and precious, you yourselves like living stones are being built up as a spiritual house, to be a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 2:4–5).

Christ is the living stone that the builders rejected, the stone of Psalm 118 that “has become the cornerstone” (Psalm 118:22). In ancient building the cornerstone was laid first, and every other line of the building was set from it. Everything else depends on it. He was rejected by men, and chosen by God.

And we are living stones. Stones on their own are just rubble; they become a house when they are fitted together on the foundation. Each believer is shaped, sometimes painfully, and set beside others. No one is a house on his own. We are priests too, offering “spiritual sacrifices”: praise, good works, generosity, our very selves (Romans 12:1; Hebrews 13:15–16). Every believer is a priest, and there is no longer a special priestly caste between God and his people.

What it says about us

If the church is God’s temple, then the gathered church is holy ground. Not the building, but the people. A plain hall with a leaking roof, where believers meet in Christ’s name, is a more sacred place than any cathedral without him.

It means presence. We do not travel to a shrine to meet God. He is among his people by his Spirit, and when we gather we meet him.

It means holiness. Paul draws the moral: “What agreement has the temple of God with idols? For we are the temple of the living God” (2 Corinthians 6:16). A holy temple cannot be a place for idols, and each believer’s body, as a temple of the Spirit, is to be kept for God (1 Corinthians 6:19–20).

It means growth. The temple is still being built, and each conversion adds a stone. It will not be finished until the end, when, as the last chapter shows, the whole city becomes the Holy of Holies.

For us

Next Sunday, as you walk into the gathering, remind yourself: God is here among his people. Come expecting to meet him. And ask whether there is anything in your words or attitudes that is quietly damaging his temple, and put it right.

An example

A church in a city centre meets in a rented school hall that smells of floor polish and has posters about healthy eating on the walls. A visitor from a grand old church says, a little sniffily, that it does not feel like a church. An older member gently answers, “It isn’t the hall that is the church. Look round at the people. God lives here.” The visitor comes back the following week.

For reflection

How does the story from the tabernacle to Jesus help you understand “you are God’s temple”? Why does it matter that the “you” in 1 Corinthians 3:16 is plural? What does it mean that Christ is the cornerstone from which everything else is set? How might you come to church differently if you believed God was really present among his people?

6.title: The Household and Family of God
6.essay:
The New Testament’s most frequent name for Christians is not “believers” or “saints” or “disciples”. It is “brothers”. The church is a family, and the warmth and obligations of family run through almost every page of the letters.

The Old Testament roots

From the beginning, God spoke of his people in family terms. He told Pharaoh, “Israel is my firstborn son” (Exodus 4:22). He is “Father of the fatherless and protector of widows” (Psalm 68:5), the God who “settles the solitary in a home” (Psalm 68:6). Israel was literally a family, the sons of Jacob, and the law was full of care for the brother, the stranger and the widow within the household of the nation.

What Jesus did with the family

Then Jesus did something that would have shocked his first hearers. When his mother and brothers came to fetch him, he looked at the people sitting around him and said, “Here are my mother and my brothers! For whoever does the will of God, he is my brother and sister and mother” (Mark 3:34–35). In a culture where family was everything, Jesus was forming a new family, bound not by blood but by obedience to God.

He did not despise natural families. He honoured his mother to the end. But he made clear that his family runs deeper. And he promised that those who lost homes and relatives for his sake would receive “a hundredfold now in this time, houses and brothers and sisters and mothers and children and lands, with persecutions” (Mark 10:30). Many early Christians were cut off by their families. The church became the family they had lost.

Adopted by the Father

How do we come into this family? Not by birth, but by adoption. In the Roman world an adopted son received a new name, a new father and the full rights of an heir; his old debts were cancelled. Paul uses exactly that picture. God sent his Son “to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons. And because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba! Father!’” (Galatians 4:5–6). Daughters as well as sons are included; in the ancient world the son was the heir, and Paul is saying that every believer, man or woman, inherits.

John can hardly contain himself: “See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are” (1 John 3:1).

What it says about Christ

Christ is the eternal Son, and by grace he makes us sons and daughters with him. God predestined us “to be conformed to the image of his Son, in order that he might be the firstborn among many brothers” (Romans 8:29). The writer to the Hebrews says that Christ “is not ashamed to call them brothers” (Hebrews 2:11). On the morning of his resurrection, he sent Mary Magdalene to “my brothers” with the message that he was ascending to “my Father and your Father” (John 20:17). The one who has every right to be ashamed of us calls us family.

The household of God

Paul writes to Timothy so that he may know “how one ought to behave in the household of God, which is the church of the living God, a pillar and buttress of the truth” (1 Timothy 3:15). Timothy was in Ephesus, famous for its great temple of Artemis with its many columns. Paul says that the real pillar in that city is not marble. It is a household of believers who hold up the truth for all to see.

A household in that world was more than a nuclear family. It included grandparents, servants, workers, guests: a whole community under one roof and one head. The early churches met in such households. They ate together, shared together and cared for widows together. “Let us do good to everyone, and especially to those who are of the household of faith” (Galatians 6:10). The family has a special claim on our love, not to shut others out, but because a family that does not care for its own has nothing to show the world.

What it says about us

It means belonging. Many people today are lonely: single, divorced, far from relatives, estranged from parents, or simply busy and unknown. The church is meant to be a place where no one is an orphan. Paul tells Timothy to treat older men as fathers, younger men as brothers, older women as mothers and younger women as sisters, “in all purity” (1 Timothy 5:1–2).

It means obligation. Family is not a feeling. You do not choose your brothers and sisters. You may not like them all. But you are bound to them, and love shows itself in practical care, honesty and patience.

It means equality. In the family of God there are no second-class children. Jesus said, “you are all brothers” (Matthew 23:8). Elders lead, but they lead as older brothers, not as lords.

And it means healing. Some come to church from broken families, with no picture of a good father or a safe home. The church will never replace a perfect family, because no such family exists. But in the household of God many have found the father, mother, brother or sister they never had.

For us

Think of one person in your church who has little family nearby: a widow, a student, a single parent, someone recently arrived. Invite them for a meal, or sit with them on Sunday. Family is built at tables.

An example

A teenage girl from a chaotic home starts attending a youth group. She is wary and sharp-tongued. An older couple in the church invite her for Sunday lunch, and keep inviting her for years. She sees how they speak to each other and pray together. At her baptism she says, “I didn’t know what a family was supposed to look like. Now I do.”

For reflection

Why would Jesus’ words in Mark 3:35 have shocked his first hearers? What does adoption add to the picture of the church as family? Why is the church called “a pillar and buttress of the truth”, and how does a household hold up truth? Who in your church needs to know that they belong to a family?

7.title: The Flock and Its Shepherd
7.essay:
Sheep are not flattering creatures to be compared to. They wander, they panic, they cannot find water on their own, and they are helpless before wolves. Yet God calls his people a flock again and again, and the picture turns out to be one of the most comforting in the Bible, because the point is never the sheep. The point is the Shepherd.

The Old Testament roots

Israel was a nation of shepherds. Abraham, Jacob, Moses and David all kept sheep, and the work of a shepherd was rough, lonely and dangerous. So the picture came naturally. “We are his people, and the sheep of his pasture” (Psalm 100:3). “He will tend his flock like a shepherd; he will gather the lambs in his arms; he will carry them in his bosom” (Isaiah 40:11). And David, the shepherd king, sang, “The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want” (Psalm 23:1). The study The Lord Is My Shepherd explores that psalm and the life of real shepherds in depth.

Israel’s kings and leaders were meant to be shepherds under God. Many were not. Through Ezekiel God thundered against them: “Ah, shepherds of Israel who have been feeding yourselves! Should not shepherds feed the sheep?” (Ezekiel 34:2). They had fleeced the flock: “The weak you have not strengthened, the sick you have not healed, the injured you have not bound up, the strayed you have not brought back, the lost you have not sought” (Ezekiel 34:4). So God made a promise: “Behold, I, I myself will search for my sheep and will seek them out” (Ezekiel 34:11). And he added, “I will set up over them one shepherd, my servant David, and he shall feed them” (Ezekiel 34:23).

The Good Shepherd

Centuries later Jesus stood in Jerusalem and said, “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11). Anyone who knew Ezekiel 34 would hear the claim. The Lord who said “I myself will search for my sheep” and the promised son of David had arrived in one person.

And the Good Shepherd does what no hired hand would do. A hired hand runs when the wolf comes. Jesus walked into the wolf’s mouth. The shepherd became the lamb. He knows his sheep by name, he gathers sheep from beyond Israel’s fold so that “there will be one flock, one shepherd” (John 10:16), and he keeps them: “I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:28).

That is the deepest comfort of this picture. The safety of the flock does not depend on the sheep. It depends on the grip of the Shepherd. And his grip is held by the Father’s hand as well (John 10:29).

What it meant to the first churches

When Paul said goodbye to the elders of Ephesus, he gave them a solemn charge: “Pay careful attention to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to care for the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood” (Acts 20:28). He warned them that “fierce wolves” would come in among them (Acts 20:29). Notice that the same men are called elders (Acts 20:17), overseers and shepherds. These are three names for one office.

Peter, who had once been told by the risen Jesus, “Feed my sheep” (John 21:17), wrote to elders in his turn: “shepherd the flock of God that is among you, exercising oversight, not under compulsion, but willingly … not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples to the flock. And when the chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the unfading crown of glory” (1 Peter 5:2–4).

Under-shepherds

Elders are under-shepherds. The flock is not theirs; it is “the flock of God”, bought with his blood. They will give account to the chief Shepherd. That should make them humble, gentle and brave: humble because they too are sheep, gentle because the flock is precious, brave because wolves are real. Ezekiel 34 is a standing warning to every leader who uses the flock for his own comfort, status or control. Where leaders abuse their position, the sheep must be protected: abuse must be reported to the authorities, and churches must never cover it up.

It also tells us how to treat our elders. The flock is to follow good shepherds gladly, so that their work is “with joy and not with groaning” (Hebrews 13:17). Pray for them by name. They carry a weight most members never see.

What it says about us

We are dependent. Sheep cannot save themselves, find their own pasture or fight off wolves. Neither can we. Pride does not fit a sheep.

We are known. “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me” (John 10:27). In a crowd of millions, Christ knows each one by name.

We are together. A sheep alone is a sheep in danger. Wolves look for the straggler. Part of the Shepherd’s care is the flock itself.

And we are sought. If you have wandered, the Shepherd has not stopped looking. You were “straying like sheep, but have now returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls” (1 Peter 2:25).

For us

If you are an elder, read Ezekiel 34:1–16 and John 10:1–18 this week and ask the chief Shepherd to make you like him. If you are a member, pray for your elders by name, and look for a straggler in the flock whom you could walk alongside.

An example

A man stopped coming to church after his business failed. He felt ashamed and assumed no one had noticed. Three weeks later one of the elders knocks on his door, not to scold him but to see how he is. They sit in the kitchen for an hour. Before he leaves, the elder reads John 10:27–28 and prays. The man is back the following Sunday, sitting near the back, but back.

For reflection

Why do you think God chose such an unflattering animal to picture his people? What does Ezekiel 34 teach about what God expects of leaders? How does Jesus fulfil both halves of God’s promise in Ezekiel 34:11 and 34:23? How can you help a straggling sheep in your church?

8.title: Vine, Olive Tree and Field
8.essay:
The Bible was written by people who lived close to the land. They knew how long a vine takes to fruit, how an olive tree can live for centuries, how a field must be ploughed, sown and watered before anything grows. So when God wanted to show what his people are for, he often reached for a growing thing. The church is a planting of the Lord, and plantings are meant to bear fruit.

Israel the vine

Israel was often called God’s vine. “You brought a vine out of Egypt; you drove out the nations and planted it” (Psalm 80:8). Isaiah sang a love song about God’s vineyard: he cleared the stones, planted choice vines, built a watchtower, “and he looked for it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes” (Isaiah 5:2). Then comes the sad explanation: “For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel … and he looked for justice, but behold, bloodshed; for righteousness, but behold, an outcry!” (Isaiah 5:7). The vine was meant to bear the fruit of justice and righteousness. It failed.

The true vine

So on the night before he died, Jesus said, “I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser” (John 15:1). The word “true” matters. Where Israel failed to be the fruitful vine, Jesus is the vine that does not fail. And we bear fruit only by being joined to him: “I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

The study Union with Christ looks at the vine as a picture of our union with him. Here notice two things for the church. First, the branches are many, but the vine is one; every fruitful Christian draws on the same life. Second, the vinedresser prunes: “every branch that does bear fruit he prunes, that it may bear more fruit” (John 15:2). Hard seasons, in a believer and in a church, are often the Father’s careful knife, not his rejection.

The olive tree

Jeremiah once called Israel “a green olive tree, beautiful with good fruit” (Jeremiah 11:16). Paul takes up that picture in Romans 11, writing to Gentile believers in Rome who were tempted to look down on Jewish people. God’s people, he says, are one olive tree, rooted in the promises to the patriarchs. Some natural branches, unbelieving Israelites, were broken off. Gentile believers, “although a wild olive shoot, were grafted in among the others and now share in the nourishing root of the olive tree” (Romans 11:17).

Then the warning: “do not be arrogant toward the branches. If you are, remember it is not you who support the root, but the root that supports you” (Romans 11:18). And the hope: if Gentiles were grafted in “contrary to nature”, “how much more will these, the natural branches, be grafted back into their own olive tree” (Romans 11:24).

This picture is the clearest answer to the question of the second chapter. There is one tree, not two. The church is not a new tree planted to replace Israel. It is Israel’s own tree, with Gentile branches grafted in by faith, and room for natural branches to be grafted back. Gentile Christians owe everything to the root. Pride towards the Jewish people has no place in it.

God’s field

In Corinth the church was dividing over favourite preachers. Paul says, “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:6). Ministers are farm workers, nothing more. “For we are God’s fellow workers. You are God’s field, God’s building” (1 Corinthians 3:9). The field belongs to God, and so does the harvest. Preachers are servants, and the growth is God’s gift.

That is humbling for leaders and freeing for everyone. A church does not grow because it has the cleverest preacher or the best programme. It grows because God gives growth through the faithful sowing and watering of his word.

What it says about Christ

All three pictures put the life outside us. The vine is Christ. The root of the olive tree is God’s covenant promise, fulfilled in Christ. The growth of the field is God’s gift. We are never the source. And yet the purpose of all this life is fruit: “By this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit and so prove to be my disciples” (John 15:8). The Son came to do what the old vine never did: to bear the fruit of perfect righteousness, and then to share his life with withered branches like us.

What fruit?

The fruit God looks for is the same he sought from Israel: justice, righteousness, love. In the New Testament it is “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23). It is new disciples. It is good works done for others. A fruitful church is not necessarily a large one. It is one where the life of Christ is visibly growing in people.

For us

Ask yourself whether you are trying to produce fruit by effort cut off from the vine, or abiding in Christ through his word and prayer. And if your church is in a season of pruning, pray that it may bear more fruit, not less.

An example

A small rural church has had no conversions for years and feels like a failure. A visiting preacher reads 1 Corinthians 3:6–9 and reminds them that they are God’s field and the growth is his. They stop measuring themselves by numbers and keep sowing faithfully: a holiday club, visits to the care home, open homes. Three years later a family of four is baptised. The old members say they have learned that faithfulness is their part and fruit is God’s.

For reflection

What did God look for from his vineyard in Isaiah 5, and why does Jesus call himself the “true” vine? What does the olive tree in Romans 11 teach about Israel and the church? How does “God gave the growth” change the way you think about your church’s leaders? What fruit is the Father looking for in you this year?

9.title: Salt, Light, Letters and Exiles
9.essay:
The pictures so far have mostly looked inward, at what the church is before God and to its members. But many of the New Testament’s smaller pictures face outward. They show the church in the world: tasting, shining, fighting, carrying a message, living as foreigners. Together they answer a question every Christian has to ask: what are we for, out there?

Salt and light

Jesus said to a crowd of ordinary Galileans, “You are the salt of the earth … You are the light of the world. A city set on a hill cannot be hidden” (Matthew 5:13–14). Not “you should become”, but “you are”.

Salt in the ancient world preserved food from going bad and gave it flavour. It was also part of Israel’s worship: “You shall not let the salt of the covenant with your God be missing from your grain offering” (Leviticus 2:13). Christians slow a society’s decay and give life its true taste, not by shouting from a distance but by being rubbed in. Salt that becomes like everything around it “has lost its taste” (Matthew 5:13).

Light was Israel’s calling too. God’s servant would be “a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth” (Isaiah 49:6), a promise fulfilled in Christ, the light of the world, and shared with his people. Jesus tells us what the light is for: “let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16). The aim is not that people admire us, but that they praise God.

A city on a hill

Isaiah saw a day when the mountain of the Lord’s house would be lifted high, and “all the nations shall flow to it” (Isaiah 2:2). Jesus says his people are already that city. A community that lives by the Sermon on the Mount, forgiving, faithful, generous, honest, cannot be hidden. In 1630 the Puritan John Winthrop, sailing to New England, told his fellow settlers they would be like a city upon a hill, with the eyes of the world on them. The phrase has often been borrowed for nations since, but in Jesus’ mouth it belongs to his church in every nation: a calling to visible love, not a national boast.

An army

Paul calls Epaphroditus his “fellow soldier” (Philippians 2:25) and tells Timothy to “share in suffering as a good soldier of Christ Jesus” (2 Timothy 2:3). The church is an army, and the battle is real. But Paul is careful to say who the enemy is: “For we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the cosmic powers over this present darkness” (Ephesians 6:12). Christians have no human enemies to destroy. Our weapons are truth, the gospel, faith, the word of God and prayer. When the church has taken up the sword for the gospel, it has dishonoured its King. The study Spiritual Warfare says more.

A letter from Christ

Some in Corinth wanted Paul to show letters of recommendation. He replied that the church itself was his letter: “you show that you are a letter from Christ delivered by us, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts” (2 Corinthians 3:3). People who will never open a Bible read the church. That is sobering, and also hopeful: the author is Christ, and the ink is the Spirit.

Ambassadors

“Therefore, we are ambassadors for Christ, God making his appeal through us. We implore you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God” (2 Corinthians 5:20). An ambassador lives in a foreign country, represents his own king, and speaks a message that is not his own, without changing the terms to make them popular. Paul could call himself “an ambassador in chains” (Ephesians 6:20): the message is not silenced when the messenger is imprisoned. Every believer, not only preachers, carries the King’s appeal to his neighbours.

Exiles and sojourners

Peter writes to “elect exiles of the Dispersion” (1 Peter 1:1) and urges them “as sojourners and exiles to abstain from the passions of the flesh” (1 Peter 2:11). The picture goes back to Abraham, who lived in tents in a land promised but not yet his, and to Israel in Babylon, told by Jeremiah to “seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile” (Jeremiah 29:7). Christians are at home everywhere and nowhere. “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20), so we hold this world lightly; yet we build houses, plant gardens, work hard and seek the good of our towns, because God has sent us there.

An early Christian letter, the Epistle to Diognetus, put it memorably: Christians live in their own countries but as resident aliens; they share in everything as citizens and endure everything as foreigners; every foreign land is their homeland, and every homeland a foreign land. That is exactly Peter’s balance.

What it says about Christ

Every one of these outward pictures is first true of Jesus. He is the light of the world, the captain who won the decisive battle at the cross, the living Word of whom we are a letter. He is the one who left his home in glory and became a stranger among us, “despised and rejected”, so that strangers might be brought home. We go out because he came out to us.

For us

Choose one of these pictures for the coming week. If salt, look for one place at work where you could slow decay. If ambassador, pray for one person by name and look for a chance to speak. If exile, ask what you are holding too tightly.

An example

A nurse on a busy hospital ward is the only Christian among her colleagues. She does not preach at them, but she is known for refusing to gossip, staying late when a patient is dying, and owning her mistakes. One night a colleague asks her, “Why are you like this?” She explains, a little nervously, about Jesus. It is the beginning of a long conversation.

For reflection

Why does Jesus say “you are” salt and light rather than “you should be”? What is the difference between the church as an army in Ephesians 6 and an army of this world? If your church is a letter from Christ, what are your neighbours reading? How do you hold together being an exile and seeking the welfare of your town?

10.title: The Church at the End: Bride and City
10.essay:
Most of the time, the church does not look like much. A few dozen people in a hired hall; a struggling congregation in a big old building; believers meeting secretly in a country where faith is a crime. But the Bible lets us see the end of the story, and there the church is so glorious that John needs two pictures at once to describe her: a bride and a city.

A bride and a city

“And I saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband” (Revelation 21:2). Later an angel says, “Come, I will show you the Bride, the wife of the Lamb” (Revelation 21:9), and then shows John “the holy city Jerusalem coming down out of heaven from God” (Revelation 21:10). The bride is the city, and the city is the bride. She is beloved, and she is vast. She is intimate, and she is a home for a great multitude.

The pictures of this whole study come together here. The bride of the fourth chapter is ready for the wedding. The people of the second chapter are gathered: on the gates are the names of Israel’s twelve tribes, and on the foundations “the twelve names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb” (Revelation 21:14). One city, Old Testament and New, one people of God at last. The city is a cube, “its length and width and height are equal” (Revelation 21:16), like the Most Holy Place in Solomon’s temple (1 Kings 6:20). The whole city has become the Holy of Holies. “And I saw no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb” (Revelation 21:22). The temple of the fifth chapter is finished, and God dwells in every part of it.

The flock is there too, for “the Lamb in the midst of the throne will be their shepherd, and he will guide them to springs of living water” (Revelation 7:17). The family is there: “they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God” (Revelation 21:3). And the tree of life stands by the river, its leaves “for the healing of the nations” (Revelation 22:2). Eden is restored and surpassed.

From every nation

Earlier John had seen this same church in another way: “a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, clothed in white robes” (Revelation 7:9). God promised Abraham descendants like the stars, and blessing for all the families of the earth. Here is the promise kept. Every language, every culture, every skin colour, every century, all together, and all crying the same thing: “Salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!” (Revelation 7:10).

That is a rebuke to every proud or racially divided church, and an encouragement to every small, struggling one. Your congregation is a tiny outpost of that multitude.

An honest objection

Many people say, “I like Jesus, but not the church.” They have seen hypocrisy, scandal, coldness and division, and the history of the church is not spotless. Those charges should be heard with humility, not brushed aside. Much of the church’s failure is real sin, and Christ himself rebukes it in his letters to the seven churches (Revelation 2–3).

But notice what the end of the story says. The bride is not beautiful because she was always beautiful. “It was granted her to clothe herself with fine linen, bright and pure” (Revelation 19:8). Her splendour is a gift. Christ loves the church not because she deserves it, but to make her lovely. To say “I love Jesus, but not his bride” is to love him while despising what he died for. The better path is to love the church as she is, because of what Christ will make her.

What it says about Christ

Everything in this study comes back to one sentence: “Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25). That is why there is a people, a body, a bride, a temple, a family, a flock, a fruitful vine, a light in the world, a city coming down from heaven. None of it began with us. All of it began with a love that went to the cross.

Think what kind of love that is. He did not love a church that was already lovely. He loved one that was scattered, stained, unfaithful and dead, and he gave himself up for her. He washed her with his blood and his word. He is shaping her now, through trouble and through joy, through faithful preaching and ordinary kindness. And on the last day he will “present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle or any such thing” (Ephesians 5:27). On that day no one will look at the bride and praise her. They will look at her and say: see what he has done. The glory of the church will be the glory of Christ’s love, shining from millions of faces.

For us

Next time you are disappointed with your church, and you will be, remember the end. Look at the faces in the room and say to yourself: this is the bride, on her way to the wedding. Pray for her. Serve her. Forgive her. And love her, for his sake.

An example

An elderly missionary who served for forty years among a people with no Bible in their language lies near the end of her life. A visitor asks whether it was worth it. She smiles and says, “When I first went there was no church. Now there are many. One day they will sing before the throne in their own language, and I will hear them.” Then she quotes, quietly, “from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages” (Revelation 7:9).

For reflection

How does the new Jerusalem bring together the pictures in this study? What does it mean to you that the city is shaped like the Most Holy Place? How should Revelation 7:9–10 shape the way your church thinks about other nations and cultures? How do the words “Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” change the way you will treat your church this week?
